question: Why can Tennessee's TVA reservoirs present a cold-water immersion risk even on a warm spring or fall day when the air temperature feels comfortable?
choice_a: Deep reservoir water can remain much colder than the air temperature well into spring and again in fall, so a warm day does not guarantee warm water
choice_b: Water temperature always matches air temperature exactly
choice_c: Cold-water immersion is only a risk during winter months when air temperature is also cold
choice_d: TVA reservoirs never experience cold water at any time of year
explanation: Deep reservoir water warms more slowly than air, so a warm, sunny spring or fall day can mask genuinely cold water below the surface, catching boaters off guard if they fall in and experience cold shock despite comfortable air temperatures.
source_note: General boating safety fundamentals (cold water immersion) applied to Tennessee's TVA reservoir system

question: What is the recommended body position, sometimes called the H.E.L.P. position, for a single person wearing a PFD to conserve body heat while waiting for rescue in cold water?
choice_a: Drawing the knees toward the chest and holding the arms close against the sides of the body to reduce heat loss from the torso
choice_b: Swimming continuously to generate body heat
choice_c: Spreading arms and legs as wide as possible to maximize surface area
choice_d: Removing the PFD to swim more efficiently toward shore
explanation: The Heat Escape Lessening Posture (H.E.L.P.) has a person in a PFD draw their knees toward their chest and hold their arms close to their body, protecting the torso's major heat-loss areas and helping conserve core body heat while awaiting rescue.
source_note: General boating safety fundamentals (cold water immersion, NASBLA-aligned)

question: When several people are in the water together after a capsizing in cold conditions, what group technique helps them conserve heat while waiting for rescue?
choice_a: Huddling together in a close circle, keeping torsos in contact, rather than spreading out separately
choice_b: Each person should swim in a different direction to maximize the chance one of them reaches help
choice_c: Removing PFDs and linking arms only, with no other formation
choice_d: Group huddling has no effect on heat loss in cold water
explanation: Multiple people in cold water can huddle together in a tight circle with torsos close, which helps conserve body heat collectively and keeps the group together and easier for rescuers to spot, rather than scattering and losing heat individually.
source_note: General boating safety fundamentals (cold water immersion, NASBLA-aligned)

question: If a vessel begins taking on water rapidly and sinking is imminent, what should occupants do before entering the water, if time allows?
choice_a: Put on PFDs if not already worn, and if possible, send a distress call or activate a visual distress signal before abandoning the vessel
choice_b: Remove all clothing to swim faster
choice_c: Wait inside an enclosed cabin until the vessel is fully submerged
choice_d: There is nothing useful to do before a vessel sinks
explanation: If time allows before a sinking vessel must be abandoned, occupants should make sure PFDs are worn and, if possible, send a distress call or activate a visual distress signal, since alerting others to the emergency significantly improves the chances of a quick rescue.
